title: Animal babies: how young animals grow into their parents' shape

summary.text: A pigeon chick hatches pink and yellow, with no grey feathers at all. Yet in four weeks the chick looks just like the parents. Every kind of animal has young, and humans are one kind of animal. Some young look like small copies of their parents, and some look very different. Your child measures how many 'heads tall' a grown-up, a child and a baby are, and finds that even a human baby is a different shape from a grown-up.
summary.art: A grey pigeon on a balcony ledge feeding a fluffy yellow chick, with a child watching through the window glass.

intro.hook: Look at a photo of yourself as a tiny baby. Now look in the mirror. Is the baby just a small you, or a different shape?
intro.text: Every animal starts small. A kitten looks like a small cat. A tadpole looks nothing like a frog. And a human baby? Babies look like their parents in some ways, and not in others. In this unit we look at baby animals and their parents. Then we measure our own bodies, with strips of paper, to find out how a baby's shape changes as they grow.
intro.art: A child holding a baby photo of themself next to a mirror, comparing the round baby face with their face now.

outcomes: By the end I can say that every kind of animal has young, and that humans do too.
By the end I can name some baby animals and their parents, like a kitten and a cat, or a tadpole and a frog.
By the end I can say which babies look like their parents and which look very different.
By the end I can say that a baby's head is big for their body, and that legs grow the most as a child grows up.
By the end I can say some ways animal parents look after their young, and that fathers do it too.
By the end I can make a guess, measure with a paper strip, and say what I found.

terms.meaning: The young of an animal are their babies. Every kind of animal has young.
terms.example: A kitten is the young of a cat. A tadpole is the young of a frog. You were the young of your parents.
terms.art: A mother cat lying on a mat with three small kittens curled against her.

terms.meaning: A parent is a mother or a father. Parents have young, and many parents look after them.
terms.example: A pigeon chick has two parents. Both of them feed the chick.
terms.art: Two grey pigeons standing on either side of a small nest with a fluffy yellow chick in the middle.

terms.meaning: A baby hatches when they break out of their egg.
terms.example: Chicks, ducklings, baby lizards and baby crocodiles all hatch from eggs.
terms.art: A chick pushing out through a crack in an eggshell, with bits of shell around them.

terms.meaning: To grow up is to get bigger and change, until you become a grown-up.
terms.example: A puppy grows up into a dog. A caterpillar grows up into a butterfly.
terms.art: A row of three pictures: a small puppy, a bigger young dog and a grown-up dog.

explanations.definition: Every kind of animal makes young, and the young grow up into grown-ups who can have young of their own.
explanations.description: Cats have kittens. Cows have calves. Frogs have tadpoles. Humans have babies, because humans are animals too. Some young are born, like puppies, calves and human babies. Some young hatch from eggs, like chicks, baby lizards and baby fish. Either way, every animal comes from parents of their own kind. A cat's kittens always grow up into cats.
examples: A street dog in your lane may have 5 or 6 puppies at a time.
A tiny gecko on your wall hatched from an egg about as big as a pea.
Ants in the kitchen carry their white young from place to place.
explanations.context: This card says that every kind of animal has young, humans included.
explanations.art: A circle of animal families: a cow with a calf, a hen with chicks, a frog with tadpoles, and a human mother holding a baby.

explanations.concept: Some young look like their parents, and some do not
explanations.definition: Some young look like small copies of their parents. Others look very different at first, and change their whole body as they grow up.
explanations.description: A kitten looks like a small cat, and a calf looks like a small cow. A baby gecko looks just like a grown-up gecko. But a tadpole has a tail and no legs, and lives in water. Later the tadpole grows legs, loses the tail and becomes a frog. A caterpillar crawls and eats leaves. Later the caterpillar becomes a butterfly or a moth, with wings. A maggot is the young of a fly, with no legs and no wings. These young look so different that people once thought they were other kinds of animal.
examples: A pigeon chick hatches pink, with yellow fluff. Grey feathers grow over about four weeks.
A silkworm is the young of a silk moth. Silk farmers in Karnataka and Assam raise silkworms.
Flamingo chicks are grey and white. They slowly turn pink from the food they eat.
explanations.context: This card says that some babies look like their parents and some do not.
explanations.art: Two rows: a kitten next to a cat and a calf next to a cow on top, and a tadpole next to a frog and a caterpillar next to a butterfly below.

explanations.concept: A baby is shaped differently from a grown-up
explanations.definition: A newborn human baby is about 4 heads long. A grown-up is about 7 or 8 heads tall. After birth, the legs grow much more than the head.
explanations.description: A human baby has a big head, big eyes, a short body and short legs. As the child grows, the legs grow fastest. The head grows too, but much less than the legs. So a child of 6 is about 6 heads tall, and a grown-up about 7 or 8. Many other young animals have big heads and big eyes too, like kittens and puppies. But a calf is born with long legs. A calf can stand within about an hour, so they can follow their mother.
examples: When you measure in the Heads Tall experiment, a grown-up is about 7 heads tall, a child about 6, and a baby photo about 4.
A kitten's head is big for their body. A grown-up cat's head looks small.
A newborn calf stands up on long, wobbly legs soon after birth.
explanations.context: This card says how a baby's shape changes as they grow up.
explanations.art: A baby, a child of 6 and a grown-up woman standing in a row, each with paper head strips stacked beside them to show how many heads tall they are.

explanations.concept: How animal parents care for their young
explanations.description: Many animal parents feed their young, keep them warm and keep them safe. Pigeon mothers and fathers both feed their chicks with a milk they make in their throat. An elephant calf is looked after by the mother, the aunts and the oldest female, who leads the herd. Some fathers do most of the work. A seahorse father carries the eggs in a pouch on his belly. Some parents leave. An olive ridley turtle lays her eggs on a beach in Odisha and goes back to the sea. The babies hatch and find the sea alone. Many animal parents know their own young. A penguin parent finds their own chick among thousands, just by the chick's call. Scientists agree on what parents do. They argue about what parents feel.
examples: Both pigeon parents sit on the eggs, and both feed the chicks.
A mother cat carries her kitten gently by the loose skin on the back of the neck.

A great hornbill mother seals herself into a tree hole with her eggs. The father brings food to a slit in the wall. Aparajita Datta, an Indian scientist, has studied hornbill families in Arunachal Pradesh for many years.

perspectives.explanation: Animal parents feel care and worry for their young, as human parents do. A mother elephant who loses her calf stays by the body and acts upset.
Parents act this way because their bodies tell them to, with chemical messages inside. These scientists describe what parents do, and do not use words like love or worry for other animals.

explanations.context: This card says how animal parents look after their young.
explanations.art: An elephant herd walking together, with a small calf in the middle, close to the legs of the mother and the aunts.

agreed.text: Every kind of animal has young, and young come only from parents of their own kind.
agreed.evidence: Nobody has ever seen a kitten born to a dog, or a calf born to a cat. Every young animal comes from parents of their own kind.

agreed.text: Some young look like their parents, and some change their whole body as they grow.
agreed.evidence: People can watch a tadpole become a frog, or a caterpillar become a butterfly, at home or in a school. It happens the same way every time.

agreed.text: A human baby's head is big for their body, and the legs grow most after birth.
agreed.evidence: Doctors measure babies and children at check-ups, all over the world. A newborn's head is about one quarter of their length. A grown-up's head is about one eighth.

challenging.claim: A baby is just a small copy of the grown-up.
challenging.for: Kittens look like small cats, and human babies have the same parts as grown-ups: two eyes, two arms, two legs.
challenging.against: A human baby is a different shape: about 4 heads long, where a grown-up is about 7 or 8. And a tadpole, a caterpillar or a maggot looks nothing like the parent at all.
challenging.context: This card is about a common guess: that babies are small copies of grown-ups.

challenging.claim: Maggots and worms grow out of rotting food by themselves.
challenging.who: What most people believed for about 2,000 years
challenging.for: Maggots seemed to appear on old meat and rotting fruit from nowhere.
challenging.against: In 1668, Francesco Redi in Italy covered jars of meat with thin cloth. Flies could not get in, and no maggots grew. Maggots come from eggs that flies lay.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea: that small animals have no parents.

challenging.claim: Only mothers look after the young.
challenging.for: In many animals, like cats, cows and dogs, the mother feeds the babies with her milk.
challenging.against: Pigeon fathers feed their chicks too. Seahorse fathers carry the eggs. Pheasant-tailed jacana fathers, found on Indian lakes, sit on the eggs and raise the chicks alone.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that only mothers care for babies.

big_questions.q: A caterpillar crawls and a butterfly flies. Are they the same being?
big_questions.hint: Inside the case, the caterpillar's body is built again, with wings. Nobody can say for sure where one being ends and the next begins.

big_questions.q: You have changed shape since you were a baby. What about you has stayed the same?
big_questions.hint: Think about your name, your family, what you remember, and what you like.

big_questions.q: Why does a baby's head start so big?
big_questions.hint: The brain is inside the head. A baby's brain grows very fast in the first years.

big_questions.q: A pigeon chick looks nothing like a pigeon at first. How do the parents know the chick is theirs?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the chick is, and what the chick does when a parent comes.

story.title: The Yellow Chicks Behind the AC
story.note: Nandini, Arul and Ammamma are made up. Pigeons really do nest behind AC boxes in Indian cities. Both parents really sit on the eggs and feed the chicks with crop milk, and the chicks really are pink and yellow at first.
text: Nandini lived in a flat in Chennai, on the fourth floor. She was six. Her little brother Arul was four. Their grandmother, Ammamma, lived with them.
Outside the kitchen window there was a big grey AC box. One morning, Nandini heard a soft sound. Coo-roo, coo-roo. Two pigeons were walking behind the AC box. One of them had a twig in his beak.
'They are making a nest,' said Ammamma. 'We will watch through the glass. We will not open the window, and we will not touch.'
The nest was only a few twigs and a feather. But a few days later, there were two white eggs in it.
Every day, Nandini looked. A pigeon was always sitting on the eggs. 'Does that pigeon never get up?' she asked.
'Look closely,' said Ammamma. 'In the day, the father sits. In the evening, the mother comes, and he flies off. They take turns, to keep the eggs warm.'
Two weeks went by, and a few days more. Then one morning, Arul shouted from the kitchen. 'Akka! Come and see! Something is in the nest!'
Nandini ran. Next to a broken shell there were two tiny chicks. Their skin was pink. They had thin yellow fluff, like wet cotton. Their eyes were shut, and their beaks were big and dark.
'Those are not pigeons,' said Arul. 'Pigeons are grey. Those are some other bird.'
Nandini was not sure. The chicks did not look like their parents at all. Had another bird left them there?
'Let us find out,' said Ammamma. 'Watch who comes to feed them.'
Soon the father pigeon landed on the AC box. The chicks lifted their wobbly heads. One chick pushed their beak right inside the father's beak. The father pumped his neck up and down.
'He is feeding the chick!' said Nandini. 'But he has no worms in his beak.'
'Pigeon parents make a milk in their throat,' said Ammamma. 'Both the mother and the father make it. The chicks drink it from inside their beaks.'
'Birds make milk?' said Arul. He opened his mouth so wide that everyone laughed.

Every day, Nandini drew the chicks in her notebook. After a few days, their eyes were open. After two weeks, little grey feathers were poking out, like the tips of paintbrushes. After three weeks, the chicks were almost as big as their parents. They flapped their wings and walked along the AC box.
One evening, Amma came home with an old photo album. 'Look who this is,' she said. There was a baby with a round bald head, fat cheeks and tiny legs.
'Who is that?' asked Nandini.
'That is you,' said Amma. 'One day old.'
Nandini looked at the baby. Then she looked at Amma's face. 'I did not look like you at all,' she said. 'My head was so big, and my legs were so small.'
'And now?' said Ammamma. Nandini stood next to Amma by the mirror. Her legs were long now. Her face was more like Amma's face.
'The chicks are doing the same as me,' said Nandini slowly. 'They did not look like their parents at first. They are growing into their parents' shape.'
Ammamma smiled. 'That is right. Some babies look like their parents from the start. Some take time.'

Four weeks after the eggs hatched, Nandini came to the window and the nest was empty. Two young grey pigeons were sitting on the railing of the next building. They had grey feathers and pink feet, just like their parents.
'They flew!' said Arul. 'Will they come back?'
'Pigeons often use the same nest again,' said Ammamma. 'Maybe one day we will see new eggs.'

Nandini turned to the last page of her notebook. She drew a pink chick on the left, and a grey pigeon on the right. In between she drew an arrow. Under the arrow, she wrote, with a little help from Ammamma: GROWING UP.
story.epiphany: Nandini sees that the yellow chicks do not look like their parents at first, and then sees her own baby photo. She works out that babies can look very different from their parents, and grow into their parents' shape.
ask: How did Nandini find out that the chicks were pigeons?
What did the pigeon parents feed their chicks?
How was baby Nandini a different shape from her mother?
art: Two grey pigeons sitting on a few twigs behind a grey AC box outside a kitchen window, with a girl and a small boy watching through the glass.
Two tiny pink chicks with thin yellow fluff in a twig nest, one pushing their beak inside a grey pigeon parent's beak.
A girl standing next to her mother at a mirror, holding a baby photo of herself, with two grey young pigeons on a railing outside the window.

games.title: Like the Parent, or Not Like the Parent?
games.context: This is a sorting game about baby animals. Each card names a baby animal. Players decide: does this baby look like a small copy of the parent, or very different?

printables.title: 16 baby animal cards to cut out

items.b: Like the parent. A kitten looks like a small cat, with a big head and big eyes.

img.credit: Apalce365, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.b: Like the parent. A puppy looks like a small dog.
Like the parent. A calf looks like a small cow, with long legs.
Like the parent. A baby elephant has a short trunk and a hairy head.
Like the parent. A baby gecko hatches looking just like a tiny grown-up gecko.
Like the parent. A baby crocodile hatches from an egg, looking like a small crocodile.
A bit of both. A baby has the same parts as a grown-up, but a big head and short legs.
A bit of both. A duckling has the same shape as a duck, but soft yellow fluff, not feathers.
Very different. A tadpole has a tail and no legs, and lives in water. Grows up into a frog.
Very different. A caterpillar has no wings. Grows up into a butterfly or a moth.
Very different. A maggot has no legs and no wings. Grows up into a fly.
Very different. A silkworm is a caterpillar. Grows up into a silk moth.
Very different at first. Pink skin and yellow fluff. Grey feathers grow in about four weeks.
Very different. Ant young are white and soft, with no legs. Grown-up ants feed them.
Very different at first. Grey and white. Turns pink slowly, from the food the bird eats.
Like the parent. Many baby snakes hatch from eggs, looking like small snakes.

printables.title: Two mats to draw on a big sheet
items: Mat 1: draw a big circle and a small circle of the same shape. Write 'Looks like a small copy of the parent'.
Mat 2: draw a big circle and a small star. Write 'Looks very different from the parent'.

rules: Draw the two mats on a big sheet and put them on the floor, a hand apart. The gap between them is for 'A bit of both'. Put the 16 cards in a pile with the baby's name facing up.
Take turns, one player at a time. The grown-up reads the name on the top card. The player puts the card on a mat and says why.
The grown-up reads the back. If the player was right, the player keeps the card.
If the back says 'A bit of both', the card goes in the gap between the two mats, and the player keeps it.
If the player was wrong, the card goes on the right mat and nobody keeps it.
When all 16 cards are played, count your cards. The most cards wins, and a tie is fine. It does not matter if some players had one more turn. If you play alone, try to beat your last count.
Then look at the 'very different' mat. Which babies change the most?

setup.art: A big sheet on the floor with two mats drawn on it, one with a big and a small circle, one with a circle and a star, and a pile of cards beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the two mats. Put the cards in a pile, names up.

setup.art: A child holding a card that says Tadpole, putting the card on the 'very different' mat.
setup.caption: 2. Turn a card, say why, and put it on a mat.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Draw the two mats on a big sheet. 3. Put the cards in a pile with the names facing up.
flow.say: Each card is a baby animal. This mat is for babies who look like small copies of their parents. This mat is for babies who look very different.
flow.kid: Look at the two mats. One is for babies like their parents. One is for babies who look very different.

flow.do: Take turns. Read each card aloud. Your child puts the card on a mat and says why. Read the back.
flow.say: What does this baby look like? What does the grown-up look like? Are they alike?
flow.kid: Hear the baby's name. Is the baby like the parent? Put the card on a mat. Say why.

ask.q: Why does the maggot go on the 'very different' mat?
good: A maggot has no wings, but a fly has wings.
A maggot has no legs.

flow.parent: Human baby and duckling are a bit of both, and their backs say so. Let your child decide first and explain.

flow.do: Look at the 'very different' mat together. Ask what these babies do as they grow up.
flow.say: All these babies look very different from their parents. What happens to them as they grow up?
flow.kid: Look at the babies who are very different. What happens when they grow up?

check.q: Which baby looks most like the parent?
check.why: A kitten looks like a small cat. A tadpole grows up into a frog, and a caterpillar into a butterfly or a moth. They change their whole body.

games.title: Who Carries the Baby?
games.players: 2 or more players. One reads, and the others act.
games.context: This is a moving game about how animal parents carry their young. The reader calls out an animal. Everyone acts out how that parent carries the baby, using a soft toy or a rolled-up towel as the baby.

printables.title: 10 animal parent cards for the reader

items.b: She carries her kitten gently in her mouth, by the loose skin on the back of the neck. Pinch the toy gently behind the neck with two fingers, like a cat's mouth.
Her baby holds on tight to her belly while she climbs. Hold the toy against your tummy and walk on all fours.
Her babies ride on her back. Put the toy on your back and crawl slowly.
He carries the eggs in a pouch on his belly until they hatch. Tuck the toy inside the front of your shirt.
He keeps the egg on his feet, under a warm fold of his belly, for about two months. Put the toy on your feet and shuffle.
She carries her hatchlings to the water in her mouth, very gently. Hold the toy in both hands like jaws, and walk slowly.
Her baby lives in a pouch on her belly. Hold the toy in front of your tummy and hop.
Many carry their baby in their arms, in a sling or tied in a saree. Rock the toy gently in your arms.
She does not carry her calf. The calf walks close under her belly, and the aunts walk around them. Walk slowly with the toy between your feet.
She lays her eggs in the sand and goes back to the sea. The babies hatch and go to the sea alone. Put the toy down and walk away.

rules: Each player who acts has a soft toy, or a rolled-up hand towel, as the baby.
The reader reads the front of a card, for example 'A mother cat'. Then the reader asks, 'How does she carry her baby?'
Everyone shows how they think that parent carries the baby.
The reader reads the back. Everyone does it the right way.
Play until all 10 cards are read. Then swap the reader and play again if you like.

setup.art: Two children each holding a soft toy, and a grown-up reading a card.
setup.caption: 1. Everyone has a soft toy baby.

setup.art: A child on all fours with a soft toy on her back, pretending to be a mother scorpion.
setup.caption: 2. Hear the animal. Show how the parent carries the baby.

flow.do: Give each player a soft toy or a rolled-up towel. Mix the cards.
flow.say: Animal parents carry their babies in different ways. I will name a parent. You show me how they carry their baby.
flow.kid: Hold your toy baby. Listen to the animal. Show how they carry their baby.

flow.do: Read each card. Let everyone act. Then read the back and act it the right way together.
flow.say: How does a seahorse father carry his babies? Show me. Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Listen. Show how this parent carries the baby. Then say why.

ask.q: Which of these parents were fathers?
good: The seahorse and the penguin.
A human father can carry a baby too.

flow.do: 1. Read the turtle card again and talk about the turtle. 2. Ask who carries the eggs in a seahorse family.
flow.say: The turtle mother left her eggs. How do the babies manage alone?
flow.kid: The turtle babies are alone. How do they find the sea?

check.q: Who carries the eggs in a seahorse family?
check.why: A seahorse father carries the eggs in a pouch on his belly until they hatch.

flow.parent: Olive ridley hatchlings crawl towards the brightest sky, which is usually over the sea. Lights on the beach can lead them the wrong way.

experiments.title: Heads Tall: is a baby shaped like a small grown-up?
experiments.context: In this experiment you cut a paper strip as long as a person's head. Then you count how many of those strips make up the whole person. You measure a grown-up, yourself, and a photo of a newborn baby.
experiments.question: Is a baby shaped like a small grown-up? How many of their own heads tall are a grown-up, a child and a baby?
experiments.predict: Guess first. How many heads tall is a grown-up? How many heads tall are you? And a baby? Will all three be the same number? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We measure every person the same way. The head strip goes from the chin to the top of the head. The height goes from the floor to the top of the head, with no chappals on, standing straight. Each person is measured with a strip of their own head. The baby is measured from a photo, so the answer is only close, not exact.
results_table: My guess: how many heads tall
What we found: how many heads tall

materials.item: strips of paper about 4 fingers wide, cut from old newspaper or a notebook
a book with a hard cover, to lay flat on top of the head
a door or a bare wall, with a few sheets of paper taped one above the other, from the floor to above the grown-up's head, to mark on
a photo of a newborn baby lying on their back, on a phone or printed. Your own child's baby photo is best

schedule.what: Guess. Make a head strip for a grown-up and for your child. Count how many strips tall each one is. Then measure the baby photo.

experiments.record: Draw three people in a row: the baby, you and the grown-up. Under each one, write how many heads tall they are.

setup.art: A woman sitting on a chair while a girl holds a paper strip against the side of her face, from chin to the top of the head, with a book flat on top of the head.
setup.caption: 1. Hold a strip from the chin to the top of the head. Mark it and cut it.

setup.art: A woman standing straight against a door with a book flat on her head, and a girl marking the door at the bottom edge of the book.
setup.caption: 2. Stand straight against the door. Mark the top of the head.

setup.art: A girl stepping a paper strip up a door from the floor, end to end, counting each step, with a pencil mark at the top.
setup.caption: 3. Step the head strip up the door. Count how many fit.

setup.art: A phone showing a photo of a newborn baby lying straight on their back, with a small paper strip held against the screen along the baby, from the top of the head to the heels.
setup.caption: 4. Measure the baby photo the same way, with a tiny strip.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess how many heads tall a grown-up is, a child is, and a baby is. 2. Write the three guesses down for your child.
flow.say: Imagine we stack your head on top of itself, again and again, until we reach your feet. How many heads tall are you? And me? And a baby? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. How many heads tall is a grown-up? And you? And a baby? Why?

ask.q: Will the baby, you and the grown-up be the same number of heads tall?
good: Yes, because a baby is just small.
No, because a baby has a big head.

flow.parent: Most children guess the same number for everyone, or guess the grown-up has more heads because they are bigger. Any guess is fine. Write it down and say nothing yet.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up sits down. 2. Lay the book flat on top of their head. 3. Your child holds a paper strip upright beside the face, with the end at the chin. 4. Mark the strip where it meets the book. 5. Cut the strip at the mark. 6. Write the grown-up's name on it.
flow.say: This strip is exactly as long as my head, from chin to top. Now we have a head ruler.
flow.kid: Hold the strip by the face. Start at the chin. Mark the top of the head. Cut it.
flow.parent: The book makes the top of the head easy to see. Keep the strip straight up and down, not along the curve of the face.

flow.do: 1. The grown-up takes off their chappals and stands straight against the door. 2. Put the book flat on their head, touching the door. 3. Mark the door paper at the bottom of the book. 4. Your child stands the strip on the floor against the door and marks the top end. 5. Move the strip up, end to end, and count each strip.
flow.say: Put the strip on the floor. Mark the top end. Move it up so the bottom is on the mark. Count with me. How many head strips tall am I?
flow.kid: Start at the floor. Mark the top of the strip. Move it up. Count each one.

ask.q: How many head strips tall is the grown-up?
good: About 7.
7 and a bit.

flow.parent: Most grown-ups come out between 7 and 8 head strips tall. Half a strip left at the top counts as a half.

flow.do: 1. Swap. The grown-up makes a head strip for your child, the same way. 2. Your child stands against the door. 3. Mark the height and count the strips together.
flow.say: Now it's your turn. We'll use a strip of your own head. Before we count, what is your guess?
flow.kid: Now you. Stand straight by the door. Count your own head strips.

ask.q: How many of your own heads tall are you?
good: About 6.
Less than the grown-up.

flow.parent: A child of 6 usually comes out about 5 and a half to 6 head strips tall.

flow.do: 1. Open the baby photo on the phone, or hold the printed photo. 2. Hold a paper strip against the baby's head. Mark the chin and the top of the head, and cut the strip. 3. Step it from the top of the head to the heels, and count.
flow.say: This is a photo of a real newborn baby. Let's measure the baby the same way. How many heads long is the baby?
flow.kid: Make a tiny strip for the baby's head. Step it along the baby. Count.

ask.q: How many heads long is the baby?
good: About 4.
4 heads.

ask.q: The grown-up was about 7 heads. The baby was about 4. What does that tell you?
good: The baby's head is big for the body.
The baby's legs are short.
A baby is a different shape from a grown-up.

check.q: Who had the biggest head for their body?
check.why: The baby was only about 4 heads long, so the head is a big part of the whole baby. The grown-up was about 7 heads tall, so their head is a smaller part.

flow.parent: Choose a photo where the baby lies fairly straight. A baby with curled legs measures shorter, so any answer from 3 to 5 is fine: it still shows fewer heads than the grown-up. The claim is: a baby is a different shape from a grown-up, with a bigger head and shorter legs.

activities.title: Guess the Grown-up: draw what each baby becomes
activities.context: In this activity the grown-up describes a baby animal. Your child draws what they think the grown-up animal looks like. Then you find out together.

schedule.what: Hear about four babies. Draw the grown-up you think each one becomes. Then find out.

activities.record: Keep the four drawings. Write the real grown-up's name under each one.

setup.art: A grown-up reading from a phone while a child draws on paper with crayons.
setup.caption: 1. Listen to the baby. Draw the grown-up.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a frog next to a drawing of a tadpole, with an arrow between them.
setup.caption: 2. Find out. Draw an arrow from the baby to the grown-up.

flow.do: Describe each baby, one at a time, without saying the animal's name. Your child draws the grown-up they think the baby becomes. 1. 'This baby is a small wriggling swimmer with a tail and no legs.' 2. 'This baby crawls on leaves and eats them all day.' 3. 'This baby is fluffy and yellow, with webbed feet.' 4. 'This baby is white and wriggly, with no legs, and lives in old fruit.'
flow.say: Listen to this baby. What will the baby look like when they grow up? Draw the grown-up.
flow.kid: Listen to the baby. Draw the grown-up you think they become.
flow.parent: The four babies are a tadpole (frog), a caterpillar (butterfly or moth), a duckling (duck) and a maggot (fly). The maggot is the hardest. Any guess is fine.

flow.do: Say what each baby really grows up into. Your child draws an arrow from the baby to the grown-up, and draws the baby if they like.
flow.say: The wriggling swimmer with a tail is a tadpole. A tadpole grows into a frog. Were you right? Which baby surprised you most?
flow.kid: Hear the answers. Which one surprised you?

ask.q: Which baby changes the most when they grow up?
good: The maggot, because a fly has wings.
The caterpillar, because a butterfly has wings.

activities.title: Busy Beaks: feed the hungry chicks
activities.context: In this activity your child is a parent bird. Paper-cup chicks wait in a nest. Your child carries food to them, one piece at a time, with a clothes peg for a beak. You count how many trips a parent makes.

materials.item: 2 or 3 paper cups or small steel tumblers, as chicks
a clothes peg, or a pair of kitchen tongs, as a beak
a bowl of puffed rice (pori or murmura)
a dupatta or towel, rolled into a ring, as a nest
a pen or crayon, to draw beaks on the cups

schedule.what: Make the nest and the chicks. Feed the chicks for two minutes. Count the trips.

activities.record: Draw your nest of chicks. Write how many trips you made in two minutes.

setup.art: Three paper cups with open beaks drawn on them, standing inside a ring made from a rolled-up dupatta on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Put the cup chicks in the dupatta nest.

setup.art: A child holding a clothes peg with a piece of puffed rice, walking from a bowl to the cup nest across the room.
setup.caption: 2. Carry one puffed rice at a time with the peg beak.

flow.do: 1. Roll a dupatta into a ring on the floor for a nest. 2. Draw an open beak on each cup and put the cups in the nest. 3. Put the bowl of puffed rice across the room.
flow.say: These cups are your chicks. They can't fly yet, so they wait in the nest. You are the parent bird.
flow.kid: These cups are your chicks. You are the parent bird. Get ready to feed them.

flow.do: For two minutes, your child picks up one puffed rice with the peg. They walk to the nest and drop the puffed rice in a cup. Then back again. Count the trips aloud.
flow.say: Go! One piece at a time, with your beak. Give every chick a turn. I'll count your trips.
flow.kid: Pick up one piece with the peg. Walk to the nest. Drop it in a cup. Go back.
flow.parent: Most children make 10 to 20 trips in two minutes. Real chicks call out for food and open their mouths wide.

flow.do: Count the trips. Then talk about real bird parents.
flow.say: You made all those trips in just two minutes. Some small bird parents bring food hundreds of times in one day. How would you feel after a whole day?
flow.kid: How many trips did you make? Real bird parents make hundreds every day. Are you tired?

ask.q: Why do bird parents need to make so many trips?
good: Chicks are always hungry.
Chicks grow fast and need lots of food.
Chicks can't fly to get food yet.

check.q: Why can't a young chick get their own food?
options: The chick does not like food
The chick is asleep all day
check.why: A young chick has no flying feathers yet, so they wait in the nest. The parents bring the food.

activities.title: As Long as a Newborn: a string baby
activities.context: In this activity you cut a piece of string as long as a newborn baby, about 50 centimetres. Then your child finds out how many newborns long they are now.

materials.item: string, wool or a thin ribbon
a ruler or a tailor's measuring tape

schedule.what: Cut a 50 centimetre string. Lay it along your child, end to end. Count.

activities.record: Draw yourself lying down, with the string baby laid beside you, end to end.

setup.art: A grown-up measuring a piece of red string along a tailor's tape on the floor, and cutting the string at 50 centimetres.
setup.caption: 1. Cut a string 50 centimetres long.

setup.art: A child lying on the floor with a red string laid beside their body, end to end, a bit more than two times, from heels to head.
setup.caption: 2. Lay the string beside your child. Count.

flow.do: Measure 50 centimetres of string with the ruler or the tape, and cut it.
flow.say: Most babies are about this long when they are born. You were about this long too.
flow.kid: Look at the string. You were about this long when you were born.

ask.q: How many of these string babies long are you now? Guess.
good: Any guess with a reason.

flow.do: 1. Your child lies down straight on the floor. 2. Lay the string beside them, starting at the heels. 3. Move it up, end to end, and count.
flow.say: Lie down straight. I'll lay the string baby beside you. Count with me.
flow.kid: Lie down straight. Count how many string babies fit beside you.
flow.parent: A child of 6 is usually a little more than two string babies long, about 110 to 120 centimetres.

flow.do: Ask whether your child's head grew as much as the rest of their body.
flow.say: You are now more than two newborns long. Did your head grow that much too? Think about the head strips.
flow.kid: You are more than two string babies long now. Did your head grow that much too?

ask.q: Did your head grow as much as the rest of you?
good: No. My legs grew more, like in the head strip test.
No. A baby's head is already big.

projects.title: The Banana Jar: watch fruit fly babies grow
projects.context: In this project you put a piece of ripe banana in a jar for fruit flies to visit. You cover the jar with cloth. Over about 12 days you watch fruit fly babies hatch, grow and turn into flies.

materials.item: a clean glass jar or a clear plastic bottle with the top cut off
a piece of very ripe banana, with the peel
a piece of thin cotton cloth or an old hanky, and a rubber band
a magnifying glass, if you have one

schedule.what: Put the banana in the open jar on the kitchen counter. When you see a few small flies inside, cover the jar with cloth.
Look closely at the banana. Can you see tiny white wrigglers?
Look for small brown cases on the side of the jar. Draw what you see.
Look for new flies inside the jar. Count them.
Draw the whole story: fly, maggot, brown case, fly. A grown-up lets the flies go outside.

projects.record: Draw the jar on day 4, day 7 and day 10. Then draw the four stages in a circle.

setup.art: A glass jar with a piece of ripe banana inside on a kitchen counter, with three tiny fruit flies landing on the banana.
setup.caption: 1. Leave ripe banana in an open jar until a few flies come in.

setup.art: The jar covered with a white cloth held by a rubber band, with tiny white maggots on the banana and small brown cases on the glass.
setup.caption: 2. Cover the jar with cloth. Watch the young grow.

flow.do: 1. Put the banana in the open jar. 2. Leave the jar on the kitchen counter for a few hours, or a day. 3. When you see 3 or 4 tiny flies inside, put the cloth over the top. 4. Fix the cloth with the rubber band.
flow.say: Fruit flies love ripe banana. When some come in, we'll close the jar with cloth. Air gets through the cloth, but the flies can't get out. What do you think will happen?
flow.kid: Put the banana in the jar. Wait for tiny flies. Then cover the jar with cloth.
flow.parent: Fruit flies are common in Indian kitchens for most of the year, especially near ripe fruit. In a cold month, they may take a few days to come. If none come in a week, try again when the weather is warmer.

flow.do: 1. On day 4, look closely at the banana for tiny white wrigglers. 2. On day 7, look for small brown cases stuck to the glass. 3. Draw what you see.
flow.say: Those tiny white wrigglers are maggots. Maggots are fruit fly babies. Do they look like their parents?
flow.kid: Look at the banana. Can you see white wrigglers? They are fly babies.

ask.q: Do the maggots look like flies?
good: No. They have no wings and no legs.
No, they are white and wriggly.

flow.parent: The maggots are very small, smaller than a grain of rice even when fully grown. A magnifying glass helps. The brown cases are pupae. Inside each one, a maggot is changing into a fly.

flow.do: 1. On day 10, count the new flies. 2. On day 12, draw the four stages in a circle: fly, maggot, brown case, fly. 3. A grown-up takes the jar outside and lifts the cloth to let the flies go.
flow.say: Where did all these new flies come from? Nobody put them in the jar.
flow.kid: Count the new flies. Where did they come from? Draw the whole story.

ask.q: Where did the new flies come from?
good: From the maggots.
The first flies laid eggs, and the eggs became maggots, and the maggots became flies.

options: A kind of worm that grows from banana
check.why: A maggot is the young of a fly. Maggots hatch from eggs that flies lay on food. They do not grow out of the banana.

flow.parent: If it is cool and there are no new flies by day 12, wait a few more days before you decide. After you let the flies go, wash your hands and rinse the jar. Do not eat the banana from the jar.

challenges.title: A Nest for Two Eggs
challenges.context: This is a making challenge. Birds build nests to keep their eggs safe. Can you build a nest that holds two eggs, even when you carry it across the room?
challenges.problem: Build a nest that holds two lemons, our pretend eggs. Carry the nest across the room without dropping either lemon.
constraints: Use no bowl, box or cup.
Use only things from home: paper, cloth, string and twigs if you have them.
The nest must hold two lemons while you walk across the room.
materials: scraps of cloth or an old sock
small twigs or dry leaves, if you have them
two lemons or two small potatoes, as eggs
general: Twist newspaper into long ropes and coil them round and round into a bowl shape.
Weave strips of paper over and under each other, like a mat, and bend the edges up.
Tie a cloth into a small sling, and put the eggs in the middle.
creative: Make a soft lining inside with cloth or cotton, as many birds line their nests with feathers.
Copy a weaver bird: hang a long nest from a string, with the eggs in a pocket at the bottom.
Pigeons use only a few twigs. Try a nest with as little as you can, and see if it still works.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own nest. Draw it, build it, and test it. Did both eggs stay in?

setup.art: A child's hands coiling twisted newspaper ropes round and round into a bowl-shaped nest on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Twist, coil or weave a nest.

setup.art: A child walking carefully across a room holding a paper nest with two lemons inside.
setup.caption: 2. Put in two lemons and carry the nest across the room.

flow.do: Show your child the problem: two lemons, and no bowl.
flow.say: These two lemons are eggs. Birds don't have bowls. How could you build a nest to keep them safe?
flow.kid: These lemons are eggs. Make a nest with no bowl. How will you do it?

flow.do: Your child picks an idea, or invents one, and builds the nest.
flow.say: Which idea will you try? Let's build it. Keep checking if the lemons sit still.
flow.kid: Pick an idea. Build your nest. Put the lemons in to check.
flow.parent: Help with twisting the paper if small hands find it hard. Let your child decide the shape.

flow.do: Test: your child carries the nest across the room. Then ask what they would change.
flow.say: Carry your nest across the room. Did both eggs stay in? What would you change next time?
flow.kid: Carry the nest across the room. Did the eggs stay in? What will you change?

ask.q: What made your nest hold the eggs?
good: The sides were high.
The middle was deep.
It was tied tightly.

items.p: Draw a line from each baby to their grown-up.
items.why: A kitten grows into a cat and a calf into a cow. A tadpole grows into a frog, and a caterpillar into a butterfly.
items.art: Four babies on the left (kitten, calf, tadpole, caterpillar) and four grown-ups on the right in a mixed order (frog, cat, butterfly, cow).

items.p: Colour the babies who look like a small copy of their parent. Circle the babies who look very different.
items.why: Kittens, puppies and baby geckos look like small grown-ups. Tadpoles, maggots and silkworms change their whole body as they grow up.
items.art: Six small pictures: a kitten, a puppy, a baby gecko, a tadpole, a maggot and a silkworm.

items.p: Draw yourself as a baby, and yourself now. Make the baby's head the right size for the baby's body.
items.a: A baby with a big head, about a quarter of the body, and short legs. A child now with a smaller head for the body, and longer legs.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the baby's head is big for the body, and that the legs grow the most.

items.p: You measure how many of their own head-lengths tall a grown-up, a child and a baby are. Who will be the most head-lengths tall?
items.why: The grown-up is about 7 head-lengths tall, the child about 6 and the baby about 4. As we grow up, our legs grow much more than our head.

items.p: Every kind of animal has young. Humans do too.
items.why: True. Every kind of animal has young, and humans are animals.

items.p: Here are three people drawn the same height. One is a baby, one is a child and one is a grown-up. Write B, C or G under each one.
items.a: B under the one with the biggest head and shortest legs. G under the one with the smallest head and longest legs. C under the one in between.
items.why: The baby is about 4 heads long, the child about 6, and the grown-up about 7 or 8. The bigger the head is for the body, the younger the person.
items.art: Three outline people drawn exactly the same height, side by side: one with a very big head and short legs, one in between, and one with a small head and long legs, in a mixed order.

items.p: Put the pigeon pictures in order, from first to last.
items: A chick with grey feathers poking out
Two white eggs in a nest
A pink chick with yellow fluff
a: Two white eggs in a nest
A pink chick with yellow fluff
A chick with grey feathers poking out
items.why: First the eggs. Then the chick hatches, pink with yellow fluff. Grey feathers grow. After about four weeks, the young pigeon flies.
items.art: Four pictures in a mixed order: a chick with grey pin feathers, two white eggs, a flying pigeon, a pink chick with yellow fluff.

items.p: Which baby does NOT drink milk from their mother?
items.why: A hen's chick does not drink milk. Kittens, calves and puppies drink their mother's milk. Pigeons are different again: both pigeon parents make a milk in their throat for their chicks.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: a tadpole looks nothing like a frog. How can we know that a tadpole is a baby frog?
items.a: We can watch a tadpole grow. The tadpole grows legs, loses the tail and becomes a frog. Or we can see frog eggs hatch into tadpoles.
items.why: A strong answer says we find out by watching: we see the tadpole change, or see where tadpoles come from.

items.p: Sowmya and Ritu, two girls in Class 1, look at a photo of a newborn baby and a photo of a grown-up.

views.says: A baby is just a small grown-up, with the same shape.
A baby has a different shape. The head is big for the body.

items.ask: Which girl do you agree with? What could you measure to find out? Then say one thing the other girl got right.
items.a: Ritu is right: a baby is about 4 heads long and a grown-up about 7. But Sowmya is right that a baby has the same parts: two eyes, two arms and two legs.
items.why: A strong answer uses the head strips to measure, and is fair to both girls.

worksheets.title: How Babies Grow and Who Cares for Them (stretch)

items.p: A calf can stand within about an hour of being born. A human baby takes about a year to walk. Why might a calf need to stand so soon?
opts: To follow the mother and the herd, and keep safe
Because calves don't like lying down
items.why: A calf needs to walk with the mother and the herd, away from danger, from the first day. A human baby is carried by grown-ups, so they can take longer.

items.p: Draw a line from each parent to how they carry their young.
pairs: In her mouth, by the neck
In a pouch on his belly
items.why: Each parent carries the young in their own way. The seahorse father carries the eggs in his pouch until they hatch.

items.p: Only mothers look after babies.
items.why: False. Pigeon fathers sit on the eggs and feed the chicks. Seahorse fathers carry the eggs. Many human fathers look after their babies.

items.p: Here is a silkworm, eating a mulberry leaf. Draw what the silkworm will grow into.
items.a: A moth with wings: the silk moth.
items.why: A silkworm is the young of a silk moth. The silkworm spins a case of silk, changes inside it, and comes out as a moth with wings.
items.art: A white silkworm on a green mulberry leaf, and an empty box beside it for the drawing.

items.p: Say it to a grown-up, who writes it down: a baby crow has just hatched from her egg. What will the crow parents do for the baby in the first week?
items.a: They feed the baby, keep the baby warm under them, and keep the baby safe from cats and other danger.
items.why: A strong answer gives two or three jobs that parents do and says why the baby cannot do them alone yet.

items.p: Sort the babies: hatched from an egg, or born?
items.why: Geckos, hens and frogs lay eggs, and the babies hatch. Dogs, cows and humans grow their babies inside the mother's body, and the babies are born.

items.p: A cat has 3 kittens. A hen has 5 chicks. How many babies are there in all?
items.why: 3 kittens and 5 chicks make 8 babies. Count on from 5: 6, 7, 8.
items.art: A mother cat with 3 kittens and a hen with 5 chicks on a farm path.

items.p: Lakshmi and Tanvi watch a pair of crows on a tree in Mysuru. The crows are feeding a koel chick. Koel mothers lay their eggs in crows' nests.

views.says: The crows feed the chick and keep the chick safe. So the chick is their baby.
The chick hatched from a koel mother's egg. So the chick is a koel's baby, not the crows'.

items.ask: Which girl do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other girl got right.
items.a: Both are right in a way. The chick is a koel, from a koel's egg, and will grow up to look like a koel. But the crows are the ones who feed the chick and keep the chick safe, so they are the parents who raise the chick.
items.why: A strong answer sees that a parent can be the one who laid the egg, or the one who looks after the baby, and gives a reason for one side.

items.p: Here is the banana jar on day 8. Label the maggot, the brown case and the fly.
items.a: The white wriggler on the banana is the maggot. The small brown case on the glass is the case, called a pupa. The tiny insect with wings is the fly.
items.why: A fruit fly starts as a maggot, makes a brown case, and comes out as a fly. All three are the same kind of animal at different ages.
items.art: A glass jar covered with cloth, with a piece of banana at the bottom, a white maggot on the banana, a brown case on the glass and a tiny fly near the top, with three empty label lines.

items.p: A great hornbill mother seals herself into a tree hole with her eggs. Who brings her food?
items.why: The father hornbill brings fruit to a thin slit in the wall, and passes it to the mother and, later, the chicks.

videos.title: Growth of baby pigeons, from hatching to 4 weeks old
videos.why: Shows in a few minutes how pink, fluffy chicks become grey pigeons.

videos.check: Found by search: "Tadpoles Development Time-lapse" by Temponaut Timelapse, 3 minutes, 46 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.why: Shows a whole elephant herd gathering around a newborn calf and look after the baby.
videos.check: Found by search: "Elephant Herd Celebrates a New Born Calf" by BBC Earth, 2 minutes, 39 seconds. A parent may preview it.

quiz.p: Which of these animals has young?
opts: Every kind of animal, humans too
quiz.why: Every kind of animal has young. Humans are animals too.

quiz.p: What is the young of a cow called?
quiz.why: A cow's young is a calf. A kitten is a young cat, and a chick is a young bird.

quiz.p: A tadpole grows up into what?
quiz.why: A tadpole grows legs, loses the tail and becomes a frog. Many people guess fish, because tadpoles swim.

quiz.p: Which baby looks very different from the parent?
quiz.why: A caterpillar has no wings and crawls on leaves. The grown-up is a butterfly or a moth. Kittens and puppies look like small cats and dogs.
Maggots are fly babies. They hatch from eggs that flies lay on food. People once thought maggots grew out of rotting food by themselves.

quiz.p: A newborn baby is about how many of their own heads long?
quiz.why: A newborn is about 4 heads long. A grown-up is about 7 or 8 heads tall, because the legs grow so much.

quiz.p: As a child grows up, which part grows the most?
quiz.why: The legs grow the most. That is why a grown-up is more heads tall than a baby.

opts: Both the mother and the father
quiz.why: Both pigeon parents make a milk in their throat and feed the chicks. They also take turns sitting on the eggs.

quiz.p: Which father carries the eggs in a pouch on his belly?
quiz.why: A seahorse father carries the eggs in his pouch until the babies hatch and swim out.

quiz.p: Before measuring with the head strips, what did a good scientist do first?
opts: Asked a friend for the answer
quiz.why: Scientists guess first and say why. Then they test, and look at what really happened.

applications: At every check-up, doctors and nurses measure a baby's length and the size of the head, to see that the baby is growing well.
Silk farmers in Karnataka, Assam and other states raise silkworms, the young of silk moths, on mulberry and other leaves.
Fish farmers raise baby fish in small ponds, then move them to big ponds when they are bigger.
Along the Odisha coast, people guard olive ridley turtle nests, so the hatchlings can reach the sea safely.

spotted.text: A pigeon nest behind an AC box or on a window ledge, with two white eggs or two fluffy chicks.
spotted.art: Two pigeon chicks with yellow fluff and grey pin feathers in a twig nest behind an AC box.

spotted.text: A tiny baby gecko on the wall at night, looking just like a grown-up gecko, only smaller.
spotted.art: A big gecko and a tiny gecko on a white wall near a tube light.

spotted.text: Ants in a line, carrying small white young in their jaws to a new nest.
spotted.art: A line of small brown ants on a kitchen floor, some carrying white grains that are their young.

spotted.text: A street dog in the lane, feeding her puppies.
spotted.art: A brown street dog lying on her side on a pavement while four puppies drink her milk.

spotted.text: Crows building a nest in a tree in April or May, before the monsoon.
spotted.art: A house crow carrying a twig into a nest high in a neem tree.

open_questions.q: Does a butterfly remember being a caterpillar?
open_questions.why_open: In one study, moths remembered a smell they had learned to avoid as caterpillars. But nobody knows how much of the caterpillar's life the moth or butterfly remembers.

open_questions.q: Why do human children stay young for so long?
open_questions.why_open: A human takes many years to grow up, much longer than a cat or a dog. Scientists think it gives time to learn, but they still argue about why.

open_questions.q: What does a chick feel when the parent comes back to the nest?
open_questions.why_open: Chicks call and open their beaks wide when a parent lands. We can see what they do, but nobody knows what it feels like for the chick.

ask_kids: What do you think a baby crow looks like?
Can you see any baby animals from our window today?
Which baby animal would you like to look after? What would they need?
Who in our family were you most like when you were a baby?
If you were a tadpole, what would you like best about turning into a frog?

jokes.j: What do you call a baby cow who won't stop asking questions?
Where do tadpoles go to change into frogs?
What did the mother pigeon say to her chick?
Why was the caterpillar not worried about growing up?
jokes.a: She knew things would turn out beautiful!

jokes.j: What is a kitten's favourite colour?
What do you call a puppy that can do magic?
What do ducklings watch on TV?
Why did the chick go to school?

maths.problem: In the head strip test, a grown-up was 7 head strips tall. A child was 6. How many more head strips tall was the grown-up?
maths.explain: 7 take away 6 leaves 1. The grown-up's legs and body have grown more than the head, so the grown-up is more heads tall.
maths.context: This is about the head strip test, where you counted how many of their own heads tall each person is.
maths.why_maths: Finding the difference shows that a grown-up is more heads tall than a child, so their shape is different.

maths.problem: Put these in order, from fewest heads tall to most: the grown-up (7), the baby (4), the child (6).
maths.explain: 4 is less than 6, and 6 is less than 7. The older the person, the more heads tall, because the legs keep growing.
maths.context: This is about the head strip test with a grown-up, a child and a baby photo.
maths.why_maths: Putting the numbers in order shows a pattern: the older the person, the more heads tall.

maths.problem: A street dog had 6 puppies. An elephant had 1 calf. How many more babies did the dog have? Which mother can give each baby more time?
maths.answer: 5 more babies. The elephant mother can give her one calf more time.
maths.explain: 6 take away 1 is 5. With only one calf, the elephant mother, the aunts and the herd can care for that calf for years.
maths.context: This is about how many young different animals have at one time.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the numbers helps us think about why some animals have many young and some have just one.

maths.problem: On day 10, a girl called Meena looked at her banana jar. She counted 3 maggots, 4 brown cases and 5 flies. Make a tally. Which was there most of?
maths.explain: Maggots: 3 marks. Brown cases: 4 marks. Flies: 5 marks. By day 10, many maggots had already turned into cases, and many cases into flies.
maths.context: This is about the banana jar, where you watched fruit fly babies grow.
maths.why_maths: A tally shows at a glance which stage most of the young have reached.

warmup.q: What is the young of a cat called?
What is the young of a hen called?
Name a baby who looks very different from the parent.
warmup.a: A tadpole, a caterpillar, a maggot or a silkworm.

warmup.q: Name an animal that hatches from an egg.
warmup.a: A hen, a pigeon, a gecko, a crocodile or a frog.

warmup.q: Is a puppy born, or does a puppy hatch from an egg?
Where does a baby pigeon grow before hatching?
warmup.a: Inside an egg, in a nest.

founder: ideas/by_topic/growing-up-and-having-young.md: the Growth Wave dance (curl up tiny, unfold to a tall stretch) is used in the Roots practice. The Nest Watch and Mammal Moms ideas became the pigeon story, the spotted list and the Who Carries the Baby? game, kept to what a city flat can do.
science: Body proportions: a newborn's head is about one quarter of total length, an adult's about one seventh to one eighth (standard paediatric and anatomy texts, and figure-drawing proportion charts).
Indian newborns average about 48 to 50 cm in length; Indian children of 6 are about 110 to 120 cm tall (Indian Academy of Pediatrics growth charts, 2015).
Rock pigeon breeding: usually 2 eggs, incubated about 17 to 19 days by both parents (the male mostly by day), squabs fed crop milk by both parents, fledging at about 4 weeks.
Fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster) life cycle: about 9 to 12 days from egg to adult at 25 degrees Celsius, longer when cooler.
Francesco Redi, Esperienze intorno alla generazione degl'insetti (1668).
Leptocephalus larvae shown to be young eels: G. B. Grassi and S. Calandruccio, Messina, 1896. Johannes Schmidt's search for the eels' breeding place, published 1922.
Seahorse male pregnancy; emperor penguin males incubate the egg on their feet for about two months; pheasant-tailed jacana males incubate and rear the chicks.
Asian elephant herds are led by an older female (the matriarch), and other females help care for calves. Pregnancy lasts about 22 months.
Asian koels lay their eggs in house crows' nests, and the crows raise the koel chicks.
Great hornbill females seal themselves into the nest hole and are fed by the male. Aparajita Datta (Nature Conservation Foundation) studies hornbills in Arunachal Pradesh.
Olive ridley mass nesting at Gahirmatha and Rushikulya, Odisha.
Moths keep a learned smell aversion from the caterpillar stage: Blackiston, Silva Casey and Weiss, PLoS ONE, 2008.
Tao Te Ching 51. Isha Upanishad, opening invocation (also Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.1.1).

roots.context: We have looked at baby animals and measured our own bodies with head strips. Now we ask what growing up tells us about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Our head strips showed a grown-up about 7 heads tall, a child about 6, and a baby about 4. After birth, the legs grow much more than the head does. So growing up changes the shape of a body, as well as the size.
deep_truth.habit: We often picture a baby as a grown-up made small. But a baby's body has their own shape, and each part grows at a different speed.
deep_truth.evidence: In the head strip test, each person was measured with a strip of their own head. The grown-up came out about 7 heads tall, the child about 6, and the newborn photo about 4.

three.who_am_i: Your body has changed shape since you were born. You are still you, in a new shape.
three.what_is_life: Every living being comes from parents, and keeps growing and changing all through life.
three.what_is_this_world: Kittens, pigeon chicks, tadpoles and human babies all start small and change as they grow. All around us, young animals are becoming grown-ups.

roots.thread: Every animal begins as one tiny cell, too small to see. That cell grows into a baby, and the baby into a grown-up. A tadpole becomes a frog, a yellow chick becomes a grey pigeon, and a baby becomes a child. One life takes many shapes, and each shape grows out of the one before.

teachings.teaching: The Tao gives birth to all things and raises them, but does not hold on to them as its own.
teachings.link: Pigeon parents feed their chicks for about four weeks. Then the young pigeons fly off and live their own lives.

teachings.source: Isha Upanishad, opening verse (also Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 5.1.1)
teachings.teaching: That is whole, this is whole. From the whole, the whole comes out. Take the whole from the whole, and the whole remains.
teachings.link: A mother cat has four kittens and is still a whole cat. Each kitten is a whole new cat of their own.

science.text: Right after birth, a baby's head is about one quarter of their whole length. A grown-up's head is about one seventh or one eighth.
Each part of a growing body grows at its own speed. Exactly how each part knows when to grow, and when to stop, is still being studied.

other_view.view: Many biologists say a body grows by following instructions. The instructions are inside every cell, and they are called genes. Chemical messages in the body tell each part when to grow.

practice.title: Curl Small, Grow Tall
practice.say: Curl up on the floor, as small as you can, like a tiny baby. Feel your breath, slow and soft. Now, very slowly, uncurl. Stretch one leg, then the other. Now kneel, then stand. Reach up as tall as you can. Feel how long your legs are now. You were once small and curled up like that.
practice.kid: Curl up small, like a baby. Breathe slowly. Now uncurl, very slowly. Stand up. Reach up tall. Feel your long legs.

ask: You have changed shape since you were a baby. What about you has stayed the same?
A caterpillar becomes a butterfly. Is the butterfly the same being as the caterpillar?
Why do you think a baby's head starts so big?

how_we_found_out.context: Some babies look so different from their parents that people thought they were a different animal. This card tells the true story of one of them.
how_we_found_out.story: For more than 2,000 years, nobody had ever seen a baby eel. Aristotle, in ancient Greece, wrote that eels grew out of mud. In the sea, fishermen sometimes caught a strange little fish. This fish was flat and clear as glass, shaped like a leaf. Scientists thought the leaf fish was a different kind of fish. They gave the leaf fish a name: Leptocephalus, which means 'thin head'. In 1896, two Italian scientists, Giovanni Battista Grassi and Salvatore Calandruccio, kept some of these glass leaves in tanks of sea water in Messina. They watched the leaf fish every day. Slowly, the flat leaves grew shorter and rounder. They turned into tiny see-through eels. The 'different fish' had been baby eels all along. They just looked nothing like their parents. Later, a Danish scientist, Johannes Schmidt, sailed the Atlantic Ocean for years looking for the smallest ones. They led him to the Sargasso Sea, where the eels of Europe are born.
how_we_found_out.who: Giovanni Battista Grassi and Salvatore Calandruccio, Italian scientists (1896); Johannes Schmidt, a Danish scientist (1904 to 1922)
how_we_found_out.when: Grassi and Calandruccio watched the change in 1896. Schmidt published where European eels breed in 1922.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That eels have no babies and grow out of mud, and that the glassy leaf-shaped fish was a different kind of fish. Grassi and Calandruccio watched the leaf fish turn into young eels.
how_we_found_out.art: A glass tank of sea water with several flat, see-through, leaf-shaped baby eels and one small round see-through eel, and a notebook beside the tank.

The sorting game now says how the gap between the mats is used and how 2 or 4 players share the 16 cards; the Heads Tall test, string baby, Busy Beaks and banana jar add up in minutes and days, and the head-strip steps are fair (own head strip for each person, same standing). I fixed the claim that the head hardly grows (it grows, but less than the legs), the fruit fly timing note for cool weather, ages of the two Class 1 girls, a repeated Redi fact and a repeated head-strip question, and swapped five weak jokes for real ones.
